lessons.title: Nutritional Requirements for Different Life Stages
lessons.body: Rabbits have different nutritional needs as they grow from kits to adults. A newborn kit drinks only its mother's milk for the first 3 weeks. After that, you can start offering small amounts of soft hay and pellets. From 3 to 6 weeks, kits should have unlimited access to a high-quality pellet feed with 16-18% protein and 12-14% fibre. They also need fresh water at all times. By 6 to 8 weeks, they can eat the same feed as adults but should still get extra protein for growth. A good grower pellet has 15-16% protein and 15-17% fibre. From 8 weeks to 6 months, feed them 1/4 to 1/2 cup of pellets per day, plus unlimited hay. For breeding does, feed a diet with 17-18% protein and 15-17% fibre. They need extra energy during pregnancy and lactation. A lactating doe can eat 2-3 times more than a dry doe. Give her unlimited pellets and hay. For bucks, a maintenance diet with 12-14% protein and 15-17% fibre is fine. Feed them 1/4 to 1/2 cup of pellets daily. For pet rabbits, a lower protein pellet (12-14%) and lots of hay is best to prevent obesity. Always provide fresh, clean water. In Africa, many farmers use locally available feeds like sweet potato vines, carrot tops, and moringa leaves to supplement pellets. But remember, pellets should be the main source of balanced nutrition. Adjust feed amounts based on the rabbit's body condition. If a rabbit feels bony, increase feed; if it feels too fat, reduce pellets and increase hay. Always introduce new feeds slowly over 7-10 days to avoid digestive upset. Clean feed bowls daily to prevent mold and bacteria. Store feed in a cool, dry place away from pests. Never feed moldy or spoiled feed. By matching nutrition to life stage, you will raise healthy, productive rabbits.

lessons.title: Types of Feed: Pellets, Hay, Greens, and Supplements
lessons.body: Rabbits need a balanced diet of pellets, hay, greens, and sometimes supplements. Pellets are the easiest way to ensure they get all the nutrients they need. Buy pellets that are fresh, smell sweet, and are not dusty. A good pellet for adult rabbits has 12-14% protein, 15-17% fibre, and 1-2% fat. For growing rabbits, choose 15-16% protein. Store pellets in a sealed container in a cool, dry place and use within 3 months. Hay is essential for digestion and wears down their teeth. Grass hay like timothy, orchard grass, or local grasses is best. Avoid alfalfa hay for adult rabbits because it is too high in calcium and protein; it can cause bladder stones. Give rabbits unlimited hay every day. Greens provide vitamins and variety. Safe greens include carrot tops, beet tops, kale, romaine lettuce, parsley, cilantro, and dandelion leaves. In Africa, you can use sweet potato vines, amaranth leaves, and moringa leaves. Wash all greens thoroughly to remove pesticides and dirt. Introduce new greens one at a time in small amounts to avoid diarrhoea. Supplements are not usually needed if the rabbit eats a balanced diet. However, you can give a salt lick or mineral block. Some farmers add a little vegetable oil to feed for extra energy in cold weather. Never give supplements without advice from a vet or extension officer. Avoid feeding bread, chocolate, sweets, corn, beans, or potatoes. These can cause serious digestive problems. Also, never feed mouldy or spoiled feed. Always provide fresh, clean water. A rabbit drinks about 50-150 ml of water per kg of body weight daily. In hot African climates, they may drink more. Check water bottles twice a day and clean them regularly. By combining pellets, hay, and safe greens, you will keep your rabbits healthy and productive.

lessons.title: Feeding Schedules and Rations
lessons.body: Feeding your rabbits on a consistent schedule helps them stay healthy and grow well. Adult rabbits should be fed twice a day: once in the morning and once in the evening. Give each adult 1/4 to 1/2 cup of pellets per day, split into two meals. Also provide unlimited hay at all times. Pregnant and lactating does need more feed. Give them unlimited pellets and hay, and check their feed bowls three times a day. Growing rabbits (kits) from 3 weeks to 6 months should have unlimited pellets and hay. After 6 months, switch to adult rations. For breeding bucks, feed 1/4 to 1/2 cup of pellets daily. Always feed at the same times each day. Rabbits are creatures of habit and sudden changes in feeding time can stress them. Use a measuring cup to ensure you give the right amount. Overfeeding pellets can lead to obesity and diarrhoea. Underfeeding causes poor growth and weak babies. Adjust the amount based on the rabbit's body condition. If a rabbit feels too thin, increase pellets slightly. If it feels too fat, reduce pellets and increase hay. In hot weather, feed more in the cool morning and evening. In cold weather, rabbits need more energy, so you can increase pellets slightly. Always provide fresh, clean water. Change water daily and clean bottles or bowls. Never let feed sit in the bowl for more than 24 hours, especially in humid climates, as it can grow mould. Store feed in airtight containers. Keep a simple record of how much each rabbit eats. If a rabbit suddenly stops eating, it is a sign of illness. Check with a vet or experienced farmer. In Africa, many farmers feed kitchen greens in the morning and pellets in the evening. That works well. Just make sure greens are fresh and washed. By following a strict schedule and measuring rations, you will save money and keep your rabbits healthy.

lessons.title: Safe and Toxic Plants for Rabbits
lessons.body: Rabbits can eat many plants, but some are poisonous. Knowing the difference can save your rabbits' lives. Safe plants include most leafy greens: carrot tops, beet tops, kale, romaine lettuce, parsley, cilantro, dandelion leaves, and spinach (in small amounts). In Africa, you can also feed sweet potato vines, amaranth leaves, moringa leaves, and blackjack (Bidens pilosa). Always wash plants thoroughly to remove dirt, pesticides, and animal waste. Introduce new plants slowly, one at a time, over several days. Watch for diarrhoea or refusal to eat. Toxic plants include many common garden and wild plants. Never feed your rabbits: tomato leaves and stems, potato leaves and stems, rhubarb leaves, avocado leaves and bark, foxglove, lily of the valley, buttercup, poinsettia, oleander, and nightshade. Also avoid onion, garlic, leek, and chives. These can cause anaemia. Some plants cause mild stomach upset, while others are deadly even in small amounts. If you are not sure about a plant, do not feed it. Keep a list of safe and toxic plants in your rabbitry. Teach everyone who feeds the rabbits. If a rabbit eats a toxic plant, it may show signs like drooling, vomiting (rare in rabbits), diarrhoea, weakness, or convulsions. Contact a vet immediately. There is no home remedy for most plant poisonings. Prevention is best: only feed plants you know are safe. Fence off your rabbit area from wild toxic plants. When collecting wild greens, avoid roadsides where herbicides may be sprayed. Also avoid plants growing near factories or garbage dumps. In many African villages, farmers use local plants like moringa, sweet potato vines, and amaranth. These are safe and nutritious. But always confirm with an experienced rabbit farmer or extension officer. Never assume a plant is safe because another animal eats it. Rabbits have different digestive systems. When in doubt, throw it out. Your rabbits depend on you for their safety.

lessons.title: Watering Systems and Hygiene
lessons.body: Clean water is the most important nutrient for rabbits. A rabbit can survive longer without food than without water. Adult rabbits drink about 50-150 ml of water per kilogram of body weight daily. In hot African climates, they may drink up to 200 ml per kg. Lactating does need even more. Always provide fresh, clean water at all times. There are two main watering systems: bottles and bowls. Bottles with sipper tubes are best because they keep water clean and prevent spillage. Hang bottles so the sipper tube is at the rabbit's shoulder height. Check bottles twice a day to make sure they are not blocked or leaking. Clean bottles with a bottle brush and hot soapy water every week. Rinse well. Bowls are cheaper but easily soiled with feed, hay, and droppings. If you use bowls, use heavy ceramic ones that rabbits cannot tip over. Clean and refill bowls at least twice a day. In very hot weather, change water three times a day. Never let water sit for more than 24 hours. Bacteria and algae grow quickly in warm water. If you have many rabbits, consider an automatic watering system. These use a large tank and pipes with nipples. They save labour and keep water clean. But they need regular cleaning and maintenance. Check all nipples daily for leaks or blockages. Flush the system every month with a mild disinfectant, then rinse thoroughly. Hygiene is critical. Dirty water spreads diseases like coccidiosis and pasteurellosis. Always wash your hands before and after handling water equipment. Keep water containers off the floor to prevent contamination from urine and droppings. Store water in clean, covered containers. If you use well or river water, boil it or treat it with chlorine (follow instructions). Rainwater is good if collected cleanly. In dry seasons, water may be scarce. Plan ahead: store enough water for your rabbits. A rabbit deprived of water for 24 hours can become severely ill. If a rabbit stops drinking, check the water source first. Then check for illness. By keeping water clean and plentiful, you prevent many health problems and keep your rabbits productive.

lessons.title: Body Condition Scoring and Diet Adjustment
lessons.body: Body condition scoring (BCS) is a simple way to check if your rabbit is getting the right amount of feed. You do this by feeling the rabbit's spine and hips. A rabbit in good condition has a smooth, rounded spine that you can feel but not see. The hips are slightly rounded. You should not be able to see bones sticking out. Use a scale of 1 to 5: 1 = emaciated (bones very prominent), 2 = thin, 3 = ideal, 4 = overweight, 5 = obese. To score, place the rabbit on a flat surface. Run your hand along its back and sides. Feel the spine, ribs, and hips. If the spine feels sharp and the ribs are easy to feel, the rabbit is thin (score 1-2). If the spine is smooth and ribs are covered with a little fat, it is ideal (score 3). If you cannot feel the spine and the rabbit feels like a soft ball, it is overweight (score 4-5). Check your rabbits every two weeks. Keep a record for each rabbit. Adjust feed based on the score. For a thin rabbit (score 1-2), increase pellets by 1/4 cup per day and add a small amount of safe greens. Also check for illness or dental problems. For an overweight rabbit (score 4-5), reduce pellets to 1/8 cup per day and increase hay. Do not starve the rabbit; reduce gradually. Encourage exercise. For an ideal rabbit (score 3), keep the current ration. Pregnant and lactating does should have a BCS of 3-4. If they are too thin, they may not produce enough milk. If too fat, they may have trouble kindling. Growing kits should be score 3. In Africa, where feed may be limited, BCS helps you use feed efficiently. You can also adjust for seasons: in hot weather, rabbits may eat less, so monitor BCS closely. In cold weather, they need more energy, so increase feed if they lose condition. Always provide fresh water. If a rabbit's BCS changes suddenly, check for illness. Regular BCS is a cheap, effective tool for managing your rabbitry. It takes only a minute per rabbit and can save you money on feed and vet bills.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feeding and Nutrition for Rabbit Farming in Africa

In African rabbit farming, feed accounts for 60â75% of total production costs. Whether you are raising 20 does for household income or 200 for a commercial meat operation, every kilogram of feed must convert efficiently into kilograms of live weight, healthy litters, or saleable breeding stock. This practical reference consolidates the key numbers, schedules, and decision rules you need to manage rabbit nutrition profitably â from weaning to breeding, using locally available feeds alongside commercial pellets.

1. Nutritional Requirements by Life Stage

Rabbit nutritional needs change dramatically across life stages. The table below gives practical targets for African production systems, where ingredient availability varies between wet and dry seasons.

Table 1: Daily Nutrient Targets for Rabbits by Life Stage (as-fed basis)
Life Stage Crude Protein Crude Fibre Digestible Energy Feed Intake Daily Gain Target
Weaner (4â8 weeks) 16â18% 12â16% 2,400â2,600 kcal/kg 60â100 g 25â35 g/day
Grower (8â12 weeks) 15â17% 14â18% 2,400â2,700 kcal/kg 100â150 g 25â30 g/day
Finisher (12â20 weeks) 14â16% 16â20% 2,400â2,600 kcal/kg 150â200 g 20â25 g/day
Dry Doe 14â15% 18â22% 2,100â2,400 kcal/kg 120â180 g Maintain weight
Pregnant Doe 15â17% 16â20% 2,400â2,600 kcal/kg 150â200 g Gain 300â500 g total
Lactating Doe 17â19% 14â17% 2,600â2,900 kcal/kg 250â400 g Maintain + milk yield
Breeding Buck 15â16% 16â20% 2,400â2,600 kcal/kg 130â180 g Maintain condition

Sources: Lebas et al. (1997), FAO; and Cheeke, P.R. (1987). Rabbit Feeding and Nutrition, Academic Press. Values adapted for tropical conditions with locally available feedstuffs.

2. Feed Types and Practical Rations

African rabbit farmers typically combine commercial pellets with farm-grown forages. Pellets provide balanced nutrition; forages reduce cost but must be managed carefully to avoid toxic plants and nutrient gaps.

Table 2: Practical Daily Ration Examples (per adult rabbit, as-fed)
Feed Component Pellet-Only System Mixed System (Pellet + Forage) Forage-Based (Low Input) Notes
Commercial pellets 150â180 g 80â100 g 0â30 g Crude protein 16â18%
Fresh greens (sweet potato vines, amaranth, lucerne) 0 g 300â500 g 500â800 g Wilt 2â4 hrs before feeding
Hay (grass or legume) Ad libitum Ad libitum Ad libitum Essential for gut motility
Kitchen/agro by-products (banana peels, carrot tops) 0 g 100â200 g 200â400 g Wash and drain thoroughly
Salt lick / mineral block Free access Free access Free access Prevents mineral deficiency
Clean water Ad libitum Ad libitum Ad libitum 300 ml/kg feed consumed

Sources: FAO (1997); and ILRI (International Livestock Research Institute) training materials on smallholder rabbit production in East Africa. Adapt quantities to local feed quality and rabbit body condition.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Toxic Plants and Feed Hazards

Never feed rabbits the following: fresh cassava leaves (cyanide â must be wilted/dried 24+ hrs), raw potato and tomato leaves (solanine), rhubarb leaves (oxalic acid), foxglove, nightshade, and datura (cardiac/neurological toxins). Also avoid mouldy hay or pellets (aflatoxin risk), and never feed lettuce in large quantities (diarrhoea). Introduce any new green feed gradually over 5â7 days. If you suspect poisoning, remove all feed, provide clean water, and contact a veterinarian immediately.

3. Feeding Schedules and Watering

Rabbits are crepuscular â they eat most actively at dawn and dusk. A practical African schedule:

  • 06:00â07:00: Fresh greens and/or pellets (first main meal)
  • 12:00â13:00: Check water; top up hay if needed
  • 17:00â18:00: Second main meal (pellets or forage)
  • Ad libitum: Hay and clean water at all times

Water: A lactating doe drinks 2â3 litres daily in hot climates. Use nipple drinkers or clean ceramic bowls â not open troughs that get contaminated. In rural settings, a simple 5-litre jerrycan with nipple fittings serves 4â6 rabbits for 24 hours.

4. Body Condition Scoring (BCS) and Diet Adjustment

BCS is your most practical on-farm tool. Score each rabbit 1â5 by feeling the spine and ribs:

  • BCS 1 (emaciated): Spine and ribs sharp â increase pellets by 30%, check for disease/parasites.
  • BCS 2 (thin): Spine palpable, ribs easily felt â add 20% feed, supplement with lucerne.
  • BCS 3 (ideal): Spine and ribs felt with slight pressure â maintain ration.
  • BCS 4 (fat): Spine barely palpable â reduce pellets by 15%, increase hay.
  • BCS 5 (obese): Spine not palpable â reduce feed by 25%, especially in breeding does.

Score every rabbit monthly and before breeding. A doe at BCS 4â5 will have difficulty kindling and may produce weak kits. A doe at BCS 1â2 will not conceive reliably.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Weigh feed daily â don't guess. A 150 g ration is not "a handful."
  2. Provide clean, cool water ad libitum; check twice daily in hot weather.
  3. Feed hay or fresh forage every day â fibre prevents gut stasis and enteritis.
  4. Wilt fresh greens 2â4 hours before feeding to reduce moisture and bloat risk.
  5. Never feed mouldy, dusty, or spoiled feed â aflatoxin kills rabbits quickly.
  6. Body condition score every rabbit monthly; adjust rations individually.
  7. Keep a simple feed record: date, quantity, feed type, and any health observations.
  8. Introduce new feeds gradually over 5â7 days; sudden changes cause diarrhoea.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â The Rabbit: Husbandry, Health and Production (Lebas et al., 1997) â full free manual covering nutrition, feeding, and health.
  • ILRI â International Livestock Research Institute â search for rabbit and smallholder livestock resources.
  • FAO â Tropical Feeds and Feeding Systems â practical guidance on local feed resources.
  • AgriFutures Australia â Rabbit Nutrition Resources â free technical notes on rabbit feeding (commercial context).
  • WOAH (OIE) â Animal Feed Safety Guidelines â international standards on feed hygiene and contaminants.

Business note: A well-fed doe produces 6â10 kits per litter, 4â5 litters per year. At a feed conversion ratio of 3.5:1 (feed to live weight), a 2 kg market rabbit consumes roughly 7 kg of feed. If your feed costs 0.50 USD/kg, that's 3.50 USD in feed per rabbit. Know your numbers before you scale.

quiz.q: What is the ideal protein percentage for a grower rabbit pellet?
quiz.explanation: Growing rabbits need 15-16% protein for proper development.

quiz.q: How much water does an adult rabbit drink per kg of body weight daily?
quiz.explanation: Adult rabbits typically drink 50-150 ml per kg of body weight daily.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe green to feed rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Carrot tops are safe and nutritious for rabbits.

quiz.q: How often should you feed an adult rabbit?
quiz.explanation: Adult rabbits should be fed twice daily, morning and evening.

quiz.q: What is the best type of hay for adult rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Grass hay is best for adult rabbits; alfalfa is too high in calcium and protein.

quiz.q: Which plant is toxic to rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Avocado leaves and bark are toxic to rabbits.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a healthy adult rabbit?
quiz.explanation: A score of 3 is ideal, meaning the rabbit is neither too thin nor too fat.

quiz.q: How often should you clean water bottles?
quiz.explanation: Water bottles should be cleaned weekly with hot soapy water.

quiz.q: What should you do if a rabbit is overweight (BCS 4-5)?
options: B) Reduce pellets and increase hay
quiz.explanation: Reduce pellets and increase hay to help the rabbit lose weight gradually.

quiz.q: Which of these is a supplement sometimes given to rabbits?
quiz.explanation: A salt lick or mineral block can be given as a supplement.

quiz.q: How long should you introduce new feeds over?
quiz.explanation: Introduce new feeds slowly over 7-10 days to avoid digestive upset.

quiz.q: What is the protein requirement for a lactating doe?
quiz.explanation: Lactating does need 17-18% protein for milk production.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a toxic plant reaction in rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Drooling can be a sign of plant poisoning.

quiz.q: How often should you check water bottles for leaks?
quiz.explanation: Check water bottles twice a day to ensure they are working properly.

quiz.q: What is the ideal fibre percentage in adult rabbit pellets?
quiz.explanation: Adult rabbit pellets should have 15-17% fibre.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe African plant for rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Moringa leaves are safe and nutritious for rabbits.

quiz.q: How often should you perform body condition scoring on your rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Check body condition every two weeks to monitor health.

quiz.q: What should you do if a rabbit suddenly stops eating?
options: C) Check for illness and consult a vet
quiz.explanation: Sudden loss of appetite is a sign of illness; consult a vet.

quiz.q: Which of these is a toxic plant for rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Buttercup is toxic to rabbits.

quiz.q: How much pellets should a dry adult doe receive daily?
quiz.explanation: A dry adult doe should get 1/4 to 1/2 cup of pellets daily.

quiz.q: What is the best watering system for rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Bottles with sipper tubes keep water clean and prevent spillage.

quiz.q: Which of these should you NEVER feed rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Chocolate is toxic to rabbits.

quiz.q: How often should you clean water bowls if used?
quiz.explanation: Water bowls should be cleaned and refilled at least twice a day.

quiz.q: What is the protein requirement for a maintenance diet for bucks?
quiz.explanation: Bucks on maintenance need 12-14% protein.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a thin rabbit (BCS 1-2)?
options: B) Sharp spine and ribs easy to feel
quiz.explanation: A thin rabbit has a sharp spine and easily felt ribs.

quiz.q: How should you store rabbit pellets?
options: B) In a sealed container in a cool, dry place
D) In an open bag on the floor
quiz.explanation: Store pellets in a sealed container in a cool, dry place to prevent mould.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe supplement for rabbits?
quiz.explanation: A mineral block can be given as a supplement.

quiz.q: What should you do before feeding wild greens to rabbits?
options: C) Dry them in the sun
quiz.explanation: Wash wild greens thoroughly to remove dirt and pesticides.

quiz.q: How often should you flush an automatic watering system?
quiz.explanation: Flush the system monthly with a mild disinfectant.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a pregnant doe?
quiz.explanation: Pregnant does should have a BCS of 3-4 for optimal kindling and lactation.
